title: Phonemes are not letters, and the IPA is not an alphabet of phonemes
trap: Each IPA symbol, like each letter, stands for one phoneme.
text: A phoneme is the smallest unit in a language that can convey a distinction in meaning. It is not a letter, and it is not even one specific sound. The IPA records phones, so [pʰ] and [p̚] get different symbols. In English both are the same phoneme /p/, because no minimal pair separates them. So the IPA describes sounds precisely, but which sounds count as phonemes depends on each language’s minimal pairs.

title: A sound difference you can hear is not automatically a new phoneme
trap: Because aspirated [pʰ] and unaspirated [p] sound different, they must be different phonemes in English.
text: Two phones are different phonemes only if swapping them changes meaning. There is no difference in meaning between [stɑp̚] and [stɑpʰ], and no minimal pair separates them in these contexts. So they are allophones of /p/. Even the English “voiced” stop in “beer” is often an unvoiced, unaspirated [p]. What makes it /b/ is its role in the contrast, not vocal fold vibration.

title: The subject is not always the agent
trap: In “The plums in the icebox were eaten by me,” “me” is the subject because I did the eating.
text: The subject is the noun phrase that controls the verb. In the passive sentence, “were eaten” agrees with plural plums, so the plums are the subject. “By me” is just a prepositional phrase inside the verb phrase. “Me” is still the Agent, because semantic roles stay the same in active and passive sentences. It feels like the subject only because English usually puts the agent first.

title: A lemma is not a finished word
trap: At the functional level the speaker selects finished words like “brought.”
text: The intended sentence was “Where’d I put it when I brought it in.” The verbs swapped, and the speaker said “Where’d I bring it when I put it in.” If the finished word “brought” had been chosen, it would have moved as “brought.” Instead BRING appeared in the base form its new slot required. So the functional level selects the lemma BRING, and the positional level supplies its tense later.

title: Spreading activation can slow naming
trap: Since related words prime each other, naming a block of related pictures should be faster.
text: Activation and selection are different processes. Spreading activation makes all the related lemmas, like duck, fish, mouse and snake, active together. In WEAVER++, selection time depends on the target’s activation relative to the total activation of all lemmas. Category feedback raises the competitors, so the target is a smaller share and selection takes longer. So homogeneous blocks are named more slowly after the first cycle, even though activation is spreading.

title: Where damage destroys a function is not where the function lives
trap: Because Tan’s lesion was in the left inferior frontal gyrus, that region is where speech is located.
text: Hughlings Jackson (1874) wrote that “to locate the damage which destroys speech and to locate speech are two different things.” A lesion study shows what behavior looks like after damage, so it tells us only indirectly what the intact region does. In Tan’s case, MRI by Dronkers and colleagues found the damage reached deep into the insula and white matter. Their other work links Broca’s speech apraxia to the insula, not Broca’s area.

title: Frequency effects are not just length effects
trap: Frequent words are named faster only because they are shorter.
text: Frequent words are shorter, so the first frequency result was confounded with length. Picking low-frequency words at random will always give longer words. The fix is to pick longish high-frequency words and shortish low-frequency words, so length is matched while frequency differs. When Oldfield and Wingfield did this, they still found a robust frequency effect. So frequency matters on its own.

title: A missing mediated priming effect does not mean activation stops after one step
trap: Because lion did not prime stripes in lexical decision, activation does not spread past directly related words.
text: Balota and Lorch tested both lexical decision and pronunciation. In lexical decision, only directly related pairs like lion and tiger helped. In pronunciation, mediated pairs like lion and stripes also helped, compared with neutral and unrelated primes. So activation does spread through tiger to stripes. The effect is small, and features of the lexical decision task masked it.
